Fast‑Anything just hit GitHub, and it flips the usual “rewrite everything in Rust” mantra on its head.

The tool profiles a Python, Node, or Ruby service, finds the tiny fraction of code that dominates runtime—often less than five percent of total lines—and uses an AI coding agent to generate a one‑function Rust crate for each hotspot. In a real‑world benchmark on an i5‑10500, a Python fuzzy‑dedupe script dropped from 4.91 seconds to 42 milliseconds, a 116× speedup.

Other languages see similar gains: a TypeScript dedupe went from 3.11 seconds to 155 milliseconds (20×), and a Go version fell from 3.02 seconds to 144 milliseconds (21×). Even compiled C and C++ code benefit, with reductions of 3.4× and 2.7× respectively when targeting the critical hot code.

Fast‑Anything records up to 500 real calls, replays them against the Rust implementation, and synthesizes edge‑case inputs like NaN and huge payloads. The port is only enabled when every test matches the original output within a tight tolerance and the Rust call is not slower per invocation, guaranteeing no regressions.

Why does this matter? It delivers Rust‑level performance without a full rewrite, preserving existing build pipelines, libraries, and developer familiarity while dramatically lowering risk and maintenance cost.

The verification step ensures functional parity, eliminating the “it works on my machine” uncertainty that often plagues manual rewrites.

What limits apply? The tool only swaps in Rust code when the performance gain outweighs FFI overhead, and it focuses on functions with high portability scores.
